title: DNA polymerase I: 5'->3' exonuclease removes RNA primers
vignette: A pharmaceutical researcher develops a novel antibacterial drug that works by inhibiting exonuclease activity during DNA replication. When actively dividing Escherichia coli is exposed to the drug, enzyme-mediated nucleotide removal in the 5' to 3' direction is impaired, leading to inhibition of bacterial growth. Which of the following enzymes is the most likely target of this drug?

clues.note: A PROKARYOTIC replication scenario - so think prokaryotic DNA polymerases I, II, and III (not eukaryotic enzymes).

clues.text: nucleotide removal in the 5' to 3' direction
clues.note: 5' to 3' EXONUCLEASE activity is unique to DNA polymerase I in prokaryotes - it removes RNA primers (and repairs damaged DNA). This directionality pinpoints the enzyme.

whatMatters: Among prokaryotic DNA polymerases, only DNA POLYMERASE I has 5' to 3' EXONUCLEASE activity, which it uses to remove RNA primers and replace them with DNA (and to repair damaged DNA). A drug blocking 5'->3' nucleotide removal targets DNA polymerase I. Answer A.
strategy: Match the exonuclease DIRECTION to the enzyme. 5'->3' exonuclease = DNA pol I only (RNA primer removal). 3'->5' exonuclease = proofreading, present in all three polymerases (I, II, III). Since the drug impairs 5'->3' removal, it's DNA pol I. Reject DNA pol III (has 3'->5' proofreading, no 5'->3' exonuclease), gyrase (supercoiling), helicase (unwinding), ligase (seals nicks), and primase (makes RNA primer).

eliminations.label: DNA polymerase III - has 3'->5' proofreading, not 5'->3' (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the main prokaryotic replication enzyme; it elongates DNA and has 3'->5' proofreading exonuclease activity. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it lacks 5'->3' exonuclease activity, which is what this drug impairs. ✅ Correct if: asking about the primary elongating polymerase or 3'->5' proofreading.

eliminations.label: Gyrase - relieves supercoiling, no exonuclease
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) introduces negative supercoils to relieve unwinding tension. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it has no exonuclease activity (fluoroquinolones inhibit it). ✅ Correct if: a fluoroquinolone/supercoiling question.

eliminations.label: Helicase - unwinds the helix, not an exonuclease
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: unwinds the double helix at the replication fork. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it separates strands but does not remove nucleotides. ✅ Correct if: strand separation/unwinding.

eliminations.label: Ligase - seals nicks, not an exonuclease
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it creates bonds rather than removing nucleotides. ✅ Correct if: sealing nicks on the lagging strand.

eliminations.label: Primase - makes the RNA primer
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an RNA polymerase that synthesizes the short RNA primer to start replication. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it builds the primer; DNA pol I later REMOVES it (5'->3' exonuclease). ✅ Correct if: asking what lays down the RNA primer.

reasoning: Prokaryotic replication (E. coli) with impaired 5' to 3' nucleotide removal
5'->3' exonuclease activity in prokaryotes is unique to DNA polymerase I (removes RNA primers)
A drug blocking this activity therefore targets DNA polymerase I
mechanism: Prokaryotes have three major DNA polymerases (I, II, III). DNA polymerase III is the primary replicative enzyme, synthesizing the bulk of new DNA in the 5'->3' direction; all three polymerases possess 3'->5' PROOFREADING exonuclease activity, which reverses one base to excise a misincorporated nucleotide (maintaining fidelity). DNA POLYMERASE I is UNIQUE in also having 5'->3' EXONUCLEASE activity: it removes the RNA primers laid down by primase and fills the resulting gaps with DNA (and repairs damaged DNA), after which ligase seals the nicks. A drug that impairs '5' to 3' nucleotide removal' during replication is therefore blocking the 5'->3' exonuclease function unique to DNA polymerase I. The other listed enzymes have distinct, non-exonuclease roles: gyrase (relieves supercoiling; fluoroquinolone target), helicase (unwinds the helix), ligase (seals Okazaki fragment nicks), and primase (synthesizes the RNA primer).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Biochem > prokaryotic replication: DNA pol III = main elongation + 3'->5' proofreading; DNA pol I = 5'->3' exonuclease (removes RNA primers) + 3'->5' proofreading + gap fill; gyrase/helicase/ligase/primase roles.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: '5' to 3' exonuclease' is the fingerprint of DNA pol I (RNA primer removal).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on 5'->3' vs 3'->5' exonuclease, RNA primer, proofreading, Okazaki fragments, or the replication enzymes? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: DNA pol III has only 3'->5' proofreading (not 5'->3'); gyrase/helicase/ligase/primase aren't exonucleases.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: DNA pol I = only prokaryotic polymerase with 5'->3' exonuclease (removes RNA primers); all 3 have 3'->5' proofreading.

keywords.front: Enzyme that makes the RNA primer
Enzyme that seals Okazaki fragment nicks

firstAid.detail: Biochem: 5'->3' exonuclease removes RNA primers + fills gaps; also 3'->5' proofreading.
Biochem > pol III (elongation), gyrase (supercoil), helicase (unwind), ligase (seal), primase (RNA primer).
Biochem > 3'->5' = proofreading (all); 5'->3' = primer removal (pol I only).

memoryHook: DNA pol I is the cleanup crew: its 5'->3' exonuclease chews out the RNA primers pol III left behind - the only prokaryotic polymerase that mops up in that direction.
